raw_response.country: Nigeria, Malawi, South Africa, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh (countries of the broader symposium project; no primary study reported in this preface)

criterion_notes.c1: The preface thematically addresses non-state provision of basic services for poorer populations across health care, education, and basic water and sanitation (listing water concessions, standpipes, water kiosks, vendors, latrine operators, and low-cost sewerage systems), though only as a brief editorial introduction to a journal symposium.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the preface broadly references institutional, regulatory, and governance factors by outlining four categories of government engagement with non-state providers (policy dialogue on legislation and standards, regulation and oversight of standards, facilitation, and commissioning via contracts and licences). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, however, Criterion 2 is not met (no) because this 4-page editorial merely lists broad thematic categories to introduce the subsequent symposium articles rather than examining how any specific rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, tariff rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure) directly governs household or community water or sanitation service access. Under both the plain wording and the narrow rule-type reading, the overall full-text decision is exclude (E05) because the record contains no empirical evidence.
criterion_notes.c3: Excluded as E05: this 4-page document is a Guest Editor's Preface (labelled EDITORIAL) introducing five separate articles in a Public Administration and Development symposium and announcing a follow-on research project. It presents no primary empirical data, no empirical methodology, no empirical results, and no systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c4: No empirical outcome data or findings on household or community water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion are reported in this preface.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this record is a non-empirical editorial preface summarizing the scope of subsequent symposium papers rather than reporting an empirical study, there is no identifiable study sample, unit of analysis, operationalized exposure, measured outcome, or empirical study design.

evidence_quotes.quote: In each country and in each sector, the focus of the research was on identifying and analysing types of engagement between government and non-state providers, and how these affect service delivery.
Retailers from local sub-networks, standpipes and water kiosks
Regulation of NSPs; oversight and monitoring of standards; supporting client information and ability to hold providers to account.
Commissioning service delivery by NSPs through contracts, licences, partnership, joint venture and co-production.

Dominique Moran locates the following articles by interrogating the existing literature on the three service sectors (health, education water and sanitation) in regard to the interaction between governments and NSPs.
The articles by Kevin Sansom (water and sanitation), Pauline Rose (education) and Natasha Palmer (health care) analyse the experience of engagement between governments and NSPs

raw_response.rationale: This 4-page publication (Public Admin. Dev. 26: 193-196, 2006; DOI: 10.1002/pad.417) is a Guest Editor's Preface / Editorial introducing five subsequent articles in a symposium on non-state provision of basic services (health, education, and basic water and sanitation) in six countries. It contains no primary empirical data, no empirical methodology, no systematic synthesis, and no reported water or sanitation access outcomes, and is therefore excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence) under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
